```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5.5)
```

This report is the integration layer. All logic lives in the services under `R/`; this document only orchestrates them, displays the results and records the interpretation. Render from the project root with `rmarkdown::render("main.Rmd")`.

```{r load}
source("config.R")
for (f in sort(list.files("R", pattern = "\\.R$", full.names = TRUE))) source(f)

require_packages(c("readxl", "readr", "lubridate", "tibble", "factoextra", "cluster",
                   "caret", "glmnet", "e1071", "kernlab"))
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(ggplot2); library(knitr)
})
set.seed(CONFIG$seed)
```

# 1. Data import and cleaning

Service 1 reads the transactions, removes cancellations, non-product codes and rows without a customer identifier. The dataset already contains `CustomerID`, so no identifier is generated.

```{r import}
imp <- run_import_service(CONFIG$data_path)
kable(imp$quality_log, caption = "Data quality log")
```

# 2. Customer-level RFM and churn label

Service 2 computes recency (days since last purchase), frequency (number of invoices), and monetary total, minimum and average order value. Churn is 1 when recency exceeds 90 days.

```{r rfm}
rfm_svc      <- run_rfm_service(imp$transactions)
rfm_raw      <- rfm_svc$rfm
rfm_features <- rfm_svc$rfm_features

kable(head(rfm_raw, 10), digits = 2, caption = "First customers (raw RFM values)")
```

Churn rate in the customer base: **`r round(100 * rfm_svc$churn_rate, 1)`%** (`r sum(rfm_raw$churn)` of `r nrow(rfm_raw)` customers).

# 3. Descriptive exploratory analysis

```{r eda}
eda <- run_eda_service(rfm_raw)

kable(eda$stats, digits = 2, caption = "Descriptive statistics (raw scale)")
eda$plots$histograms
eda$plots$densities
eda$plots$churn_bar
eda$plots$frequency_bar
kable(eda$outliers, digits = 1, caption = "Outliers by the 1.5 x IQR rule")

save_artifact(eda$plots$histograms, "eda_histograms.png")
save_artifact(eda$plots$densities,  "eda_densities.png")
save_artifact(eda$plots$churn_bar,  "eda_churn_bar.png")
save_artifact(eda$plots$frequency_bar, "eda_frequency_bar.png")
```

**Key findings**

- The churn rate is **`r round(100 * eda$churn_rate, 1)`%**.
- Every monetary and frequency variable is strongly right-skewed. The mean is pulled well above the median, which is why the log1p transform is applied before clustering and modelling.
- Outliers are concentrated in the upper tail of frequency and spend (`r max(eda$outliers$outlier_pct)`% at most for any variable). These are most likely wholesale accounts. They are kept because they are real business customers, but they dominate the variance and are a reason to use log scales.

# 4. Clustering: K-means and hierarchical

Service 4 standardises the five RFM variables with `scale()`, runs K-means with the initial k = 3, selects the optimal k using the elbow method and the average silhouette width, and retrains. Hierarchical clustering uses Ward.D2 on the same distance matrix.

```{r clustering}
clu <- run_clustering_service(rfm_features, rfm_raw)

cat("Optimal k (K-means, silhouette):", clu$k_optimal_kmeans, "\n")
cat("Optimal k (hierarchical, silhouette):", clu$k_optimal_hclust, "\n")

clu$plots$elbow
clu$plots$silhouette
clu$plots$dendrogram
clu$plots$scatter_frequency_spend
clu$plots$scatter_recency_frequency

kable(clu$crosstab, caption = "Cluster agreement: K-means vs hierarchical")
kable(clu$profiles$kmeans, caption = "K-means segment profiles (raw scale)")
kable(clu$profiles$hclust, caption = "Hierarchical segment profiles (raw scale)")

save_artifact(clu$plots$elbow, "clust_elbow.png")
save_artifact(clu$plots$silhouette, "clust_silhouette.png")
save_artifact(clu$plots$dendrogram, "clust_dendrogram.png")
save_artifact(clu$plots$scatter_frequency_spend, "clust_scatter_freq_spend.png")
save_artifact(clu$plots$scatter_recency_frequency, "clust_scatter_rec_freq.png")
```

**Segment interpretation**

*[Analyst commentary: describe each K-means segment using the profile table, covering size, average order value, recency and churn rate. Then state how well the hierarchical solution agrees with it, using the cross-tab.]*

# 5. Churn classification: logistic regression and SVM

Service 5 splits the data 70/30 with stratification on the churn label, so both sets keep the same churn ratio. Recency is excluded from the predictors because it defines the label (see the leakage note in the service file).

```{r classification}
clf <- run_classification_service(rfm_features)

kable(clf$class_balance, digits = 2, caption = "Churn ratio in train and test sets")

kable(clf$evaluations$logistic$confusion, caption = "Confusion matrix: logistic regression (test)")
kable(clf$evaluations$svm$confusion, caption = "Confusion matrix: SVM radial (test)")

kable(clf$metrics, digits = 3, caption = "Test-set performance, baseline models")
cat("Best balance between false positives and false negatives:", clf$best, "\n")
```

**Interpretation**

*[Analyst commentary: compare the false positive and false negative counts of the two models. Explain which one better balances the two error types and why this matters for retention, since a false negative is a churner who goes unnoticed and a false positive is a loyal customer who receives an unnecessary retention offer.]*

# 6. 10-fold cross-validation

Service 6 runs 10-fold cross-validation for both models and extracts accuracy, recall and F1 for every fold with `resamples()`.

```{r cv}
cvs <- run_cv_service(clf$split$train)

kable(cvs$fold_table, digits = 3, caption = "Mean and SD of metrics across the 10 folds")
cat("Most stable model (lowest SD of F1):", cvs$stability, "\n")

bwplot_obj <- lattice::bwplot(cvs$resamples, metric = c("Accuracy", "Recall", "F1"))
print(bwplot_obj)
```

**Stability**

*[Analyst commentary: say whether the metrics vary substantially across folds (look at the SD values and the box plots), and which model is more consistent.]*

# 7. Hyperparameter tuning and final evaluation

Service 7 tunes glmnet (alpha and lambda) and the radial SVM (sigma and C) with 5-fold CV repeated 3 times, selecting on F1. The tuned models are then evaluated on the same test set used in Section 5.

```{r tuning, cache = TRUE}
tun <- run_tuning_service(clf$split$train, clf$split$test, baseline_metrics = clf$metrics)

cat("Best glmnet parameters: alpha =", tun$best_params$logistic$alpha,
    ", lambda =", signif(tun$best_params$logistic$lambda, 3), "\n")
cat("Best SVM parameters: sigma =", tun$best_params$svm$sigma,
    ", C =", tun$best_params$svm$C, "\n")

kable(tun$tuned_metrics, digits = 3, caption = "Test-set performance, tuned models")
kable(tun$gains, digits = 3, caption = "Gains from tuning (tuned minus baseline)")

plot(tun$fits$svm)
plot(tun$fits$logistic)
```

**Reflection and recommendation**

Tuned models achieve the following F1 on the test set: logistic regression **`r round(tun$tuned_metrics$f1[1], 3)`** and radial SVM **`r round(tun$tuned_metrics$f1[2], 3)`**. The recommended model for deployment, based on test F1, is **`r tun$recommendation`**.

*[Analyst commentary: judge whether tuning produced a real gain, or whether the gain is within the fold-to-fold variation seen in Section 6. Then give the deployment recommendation and its main caveat.]*

# 8. Summary

| Stage | Output |
|---|---|
| Customers analysed | `r nrow(rfm_raw)` |
| Churn rate | `r round(100 * rfm_svc$churn_rate, 1)`% |
| Optimal k (K-means / hierarchical) | `r clu$k_optimal_kmeans` / `r clu$k_optimal_hclust` |
| Best baseline model (test) | `r clf$best` |
| Most stable model (CV) | `r cvs$stability` |
| Recommended model (tuned) | `r tun$recommendation` |

```{r save-results}
save_artifact(clf$metrics, "classification_baseline_metrics.csv")
save_artifact(tun$tuned_metrics, "classification_tuned_metrics.csv")
save_artifact(cvs$fold_table, "cv_fold_summary.csv")
save_artifact(rfm_raw, "rfm_customers.csv")
```
